hook_text: Why does the second matchstick square need only 3 matches?
clip_script: One square needs four matches. Two squares in a row share a side, so they need seven matches. Three squares need ten. Four squares need thirteen. Each term is three more than the previous. The diagram explains the difference. Each new square shares one side with the previous square, so it needs only three new matches, not four.
visual_style: Matches snap into a row of squares; the shared side of each new square glows; a counter ticks 4, 7, 10, 13.
pacing: One square at a time, then a quick jump to 10 squares.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to predict any matchstick pattern without building it.
